notes.text: An old measure of distance. Verne uses the French metric league of 4 kilometers (about 2.5 miles), and a 'nautical league' of three nautical miles, about 5.5 kilometers. The title's twenty thousand leagues is a distance traveled under the seas, not a depth: no ocean is more than a few leagues deep.

The scientific name for whales, dolphins and porpoises: mammals that live in the sea but breathe air through blowholes. Calling the mystery object a cetacean is the scientists' first guess at what it is, which is why the jets of water and the 'blowing' in the reports matter so much to them.

Real naturalists of the Paris Museum of Natural History. Georges Cuvier (d. 1832) founded comparative anatomy and the study of fossils; Lacépède wrote the standard natural history of fish; Duméril and Quatrefages were working zoologists in the 1860s. They stand for the French scientific establishment, and the narrator's own colleagues.

notes.term: latitude, longitude and the meridian of Greenwich
notes.text: Latitude is degrees north or south of the equator; longitude is degrees east or west of a chosen 'prime meridian'. In 1866 there was no agreed one: British and American charts counted from Greenwich, French ones from Paris. Greenwich became the world standard only in 1884, so the book's positions shift between the two.
notes.quote: west of the meridian of Greenwich

notes.text: A ship's speed in nautical miles per hour; a nautical mile is 1,852 meters, a little longer than a land mile. The Moravian's thirteen knots is about 15 miles per hour, a good speed for an 1860s liner. The narrator switches freely between knots and miles per hour.
A sailor's short distance, roughly a tenth of a nautical mile (about 185–200 meters), named after the length of a ship's anchor cable. Three cable lengths is close enough to see the water churning.

Facing the bow (front) of a ship, starboard is the right-hand side and port the left. The quarter is the rear part of either side, near the stern. So the Moravian was struck at the back of its right-hand side.
notes.quote: ran its starboard quarter afoul of a rock

notes.text: The kraken was a Norwegian legend of a sea monster so huge it could be mistaken for an island; Bishop Erik Pontoppidan wrote it up in his Natural History of Norway (1752–53). The Egede family of missionaries in Greenland reported a giant sea serpent in 1734. Sea-serpent sightings by sailors were still taken half-seriously in the 1860s.
notes.quote: the Norwegian stories of Bishop Pontoppidan

notes.text: Samuel Cunard's line really did start a Liverpool–Halifax mail service in 1840, and its record for safety was famous. The Scotia was a real Cunard paddle steamer, launched in 1861. The Great Eastern, Brunel's iron giant of 1858, was by far the largest ship afloat, five times the size of anything else.
notes.quote: after the Great Eastern, the biggest ever to plow the seas

notes.text: Patches or trails of sea that glow at night, caused by swarms of tiny light-making organisms such as plankton, salps and jellyfish. Sailors knew it well, which is why a glow in the reports seems natural at first.
notes.quote: sometimes giving off a phosphorescent glow

notes.text: The Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle, France's leading natural-history institution, stands in the Jardin des Plantes (the 'Botanical Gardens') on the Left Bank of Paris, with its own zoo. An assistant professor there was a serious scientist; Aronnax lives in its little world of collections and specimens.
notes.quote: Assistant Professor at the Paris Museum of Natural History

notes.text: Eroded, barren country in the American West, rich in fossils of extinct mammals. In the 1850s–60s it drew fossil-hunting expeditions, which is why a French naturalist would come home 'laden with valuable collections' of bones.

The Chassepot was the French army's new breech-loading rifle, adopted in 1866, a symbol of the arms race of the day. 'Torpedo' then meant any underwater explosive, including moored mines; the first self-propelled torpedo was built in 1866. Aronnax sees weapons getting steadily more terrible.
notes.quote: The Chassepot rifle led to the torpedo

notes.text: The USS Monitor, a Union ironclad of the American Civil War, famous for its 1862 duel with the Confederate ironclad Virginia. It rode so low in the water that it looked half-submerged, and 'monitor' became the name for that whole class of armored warship.

A large book format, made by folding each printed sheet twice to give four leaves. A two-volume quarto was a weighty, expensive scholarly work, so the phrase is Aronnax's way of signaling his authority (and, a little, his vanity).

The narwhal (Verne's spelling, narwhale) is an Arctic whale whose males grow a single straight, spiral tusk, actually a tooth, up to about three meters long. Its tusks were sold for centuries as 'unicorn horns', hence 'sea unicorn'. Real narwhals are about five meters long, not the twenty meters Aronnax claims, and do not ram ships.
notes.quote: The common narwhale, or sea unicorn

notes.text: Steam warships of the 1860s were often built with a reinforced, pointed prow, or 'spur', meant to smash enemy hulls below the waterline. Ramming seemed the coming tactic after the Austrian fleet sank an Italian ironclad that way at the Battle of Lissa in 1866.

The first lasting telegraph cable under the Atlantic, laid by the Great Eastern in 1866, letting news cross between Europe and America in minutes instead of ten days by ship. In 1867 it was still a marvel, hence the joke about the monster intercepting telegrams.

In the 1860s, a fast warship with both steam engines and a full set of masts and sails, smaller than a battleship and built for speed and independent cruising. The Abraham Lincoln is fictional, named for the president assassinated only two years earlier.
notes.quote: A high-speed frigate, the Abraham Lincoln

notes.text: A fictional officer, but readers of 1870 would hear the name of David Farragut, the Civil War hero who became the US Navy's first full admiral in 1866, famous for 'Damn the torpedoes!' at Mobile Bay. Verne borrows the name as shorthand for American naval daring.
notes.quote: The naval arsenals were unlocked for Commander Farragut

notes.text: The long-sought sea route from the Atlantic to the Pacific through the Arctic islands north of Canada. Centuries of expeditions failed, and Sir John Franklin's vanished with all hands in the 1840s; it was proverbial for a hopeless, deadly quest.
The opposite side of the globe, especially Australia and New Zealand as seen from Europe. Going home to France by way of the Antipodes means going the long way round the world.

The ranked system of sorting living things begun by Linnaeus: here branch, class, order, family, genus, species, variety. 'Branch' is Cuvier's top division (roughly today's phylum), such as vertebrates or mollusks. Conseil can recite the whole ladder but can't recognize the animals themselves, a running joke.
notes.quote: branches, groups, classes, subclasses, orders, families

notes.text: From Flanders, the Dutch-speaking north of Belgium and a corner of northern France. Flemings had a reputation for steadiness and hard work, and their language is close to German.

Formal French servants spoke to employers as 'Monsieur' in the third person ('Does Monsieur wish...'), rendered here as 'master'. Even in 1867 it was old-fashioned, and Conseil keeps it up in the most absurd situations; the comedy is in the contrast.

The first are fossil mammals from the American West: archaeotherium a huge pig-like beast, hyracotherium the fox-sized ancestor of the horse, oreodonts sheep-sized grazers. The babirusa is very much alive: a wild pig from Indonesia whose tusks curl up through its snout.

A gold twenty-franc coin (a 'napoleon') was about five or six days' pay for a French laborer of the 1860s, who earned three or four francs a day. It's a lavish cab fare, paid by a man in a great hurry.
notes.quote: For a fare of twenty francs

notes.text: A unit of pressure equal to the weight of the air at sea level, about one kilogram on every square centimeter. Boiler steam was measured in atmospheres; so is water pressure, which adds one atmosphere for roughly every ten meters (32 feet) of depth.
The American flag of 1867 had thirty-seven stars, Nebraska having joined the Union that March. Verne's thirty-nine is a slip; a 39-star flag never officially existed.

Windward is the side the wind blows from; leeward (said 'loo-ard') is the side it blows toward, the sheltered side. The harbor pilot's schooner waits to leeward of the frigate; 'to leeward of the coast' means downwind of it.
The monstrous sea creature in the Book of Job (chapter 41), whom no man can catch with a hook. Farragut believes in the narwhal the way the devout believe in leviathan: on faith.
notes.quote: the leviathan from the Book of Job

notes.text: The Knights Hospitaller ruled the island of Rhodes from 1310 to 1522. Legend says one of them, Dieudonné de Gozon, killed a dragon that was ravaging the island in the 1340s and later became Grand Master. Farragut is a crusader with a single foe.
notes.quote: a latter-day Sir Dieudonné of Gozo

notes.text: Crosstrees are short timbers near a mast's top where a lookout can perch; the topgallant is the third sail up from the deck. Volunteering to stand watch up there, in all weather, shows how badly the crew want the prize.
notes.quote: the crosstrees of the topgallant sail

notes.text: A huge sum to a sailor. An American seaman of the 1860s earned perhaps $15–25 a month, so the reward was close to a decade's wages, roughly the price of a comfortable house. No wonder the masts are crowded.
In Greek myth, Argus Panoptes was a giant with a hundred eyes, some always open, set by Hera to keep watch. A ship full of lookouts deserves the name.

The world's fair held in Paris from April to November 1867, where nations showed off their latest machines and weapons, including huge Krupp cannon. Verne visited it and used its displays of technology for this book.

Québécois French kept many words and sounds of the 16th–17th-century French of the first settlers, the language of Rabelais's era. Quebec was French until Britain took it in 1763, so a French Canadian like Ned and a Parisian can talk, though each finds the other's French quaint.

The octopus (French 'poulpe' or 'pieuvre'). Victor Hugo's Toilers of the Sea (1866) had just made a man-killing devilfish famous. Aronnax's point is that it's a mollusk ('soft one', from Latin mollis), with no bones to drive a weapon through iron.

François Arago (1786–1853), astronomer, physicist and politician, director of the Paris Observatory and one of the most famous French scientists of the century. His name stands for French science generally.
notes.quote: a famous catchphrase of the scientist Arago

notes.text: New England whaling fleets hunted the world's oceans for whale oil (for lamps and machinery) and baleen; the trade peaked around 1850 and was declining by 1867 as petroleum took over. A whaling crew would welcome a harpooner of Ned's fame.
A hunter's term for bringing down two birds with the two barrels of a shotgun, one after the other. Ned does it with whales and a hand harpoon.

Cape Horn is the southern tip of South America, notorious for storms. Before the Panama Canal (1914), ships between the Atlantic and Pacific had to round it ('double' it) or thread the narrow Strait of Magellan farther north.
notes.quote: maneuvered instead to double Cape Horn

notes.text: Verne uses it to mean able to see in the dark. Confusingly, modern medicine uses 'nyctalopia' for the opposite, night blindness.
A popular story says that in October 1492, facing a near-mutiny, Columbus begged his crew for three more days before turning back, and land was sighted in time. Farragut makes the same bargain.
Short for boatswain: the senior petty officer in charge of rigging, anchors and the deck crew. He speaks for the ordinary sailors' common sense.
A measure of depth equal to six feet (1.83 meters), roughly the span of a man's outstretched arms. Sailors sounded the depth in fathoms with a weighted line.

Fish that stun prey with electric shocks: the South American electric eel can discharge several hundred volts, the torpedo ray less. In the 1860s they were the only known animal sources of electricity, so an 'electric narwhal' sounds just about possible.
notes.quote: an electric eel or an electric ray

notes.text: The old way to measure speed: a wooden float on a line knotted at fixed intervals was thrown astern, and sailors counted how many knots ran out in a set time. That is where the 'knot' comes from.

The bowsprit is the spar jutting forward from a ship's bow; bobstays and the martingale are the chains and struts bracing it from below. Perched there, Ned hangs out over the water ahead of the ship, the nearest point to the quarry.
notes.quote: perch on the bobstays under the bowsprit

notes.text: Pushing a boiler past its rated pressure risked blowing it apart, and American river steamboats were notorious for doing so in races: hundreds died in Mississippi boiler explosions, most famously the Sultana in 1865. Hence Aronnax's fear of being blown skyhigh.

Lord Byron famously swam the Hellespont, the strait between Europe and Asia, in 1810 in imitation of the legend of Leander. Edgar Allan Poe, as a boy, swam six miles up the James River in Virginia. Aronnax is joking about his modest place among 'authors'.
notes.quote: such other authors as Byron and Edgar Allan Poe

notes.text: The biblical prophet who was swallowed by a great fish and lived three days in its belly before being cast up alive. Aronnax dismisses the idea that the voice could come from inside the beast.
notes.quote: Gone are the days when Jonahs took refuge

notes.text: Real underwater boats of the time were crude and deadly. The Confederate H. L. Hunley sank a Union ship in 1864 and was lost with its crew; the French Plongeur (1863), driven by compressed air, could barely hold its depth. Robert Fulton had built one for Napoleon in 1800. Nothing remotely like a fast, armored, long-range submarine existed.

Iron ships of the period were built from metal sheets overlapped and joined with rows of hot-driven rivets, like boilers (hence 'boilerplate'). The neat lines of rivets are what tell Aronnax the 'animal' was built.

An island in the southwest Pacific annexed by France in 1853 and made a penal colony in 1864. Europeans of the time routinely called its Kanak people cannibal 'savages'; Ned's remark reflects that period prejudice.

The sunny region of southeastern France around Marseilles. Northern Frenchmen stereotyped Provençals as stocky, exuberant and endlessly talkative, which is the joke when this man says nothing Aronnax can understand.

The belief, hugely popular in the 18th and 19th centuries, that character can be read from the face and body; Gratiolet was a French anatomist and Engel a German writer on gesture. It is now regarded as pseudoscience, like the palmistry Aronnax also invokes.
notes.quote: physiognomists, those analysts of facial character

notes.text: Latin, 'you shall have the body': the legal writ by which a prisoner must be brought before a court to test whether he is lawfully held. A cornerstone of English and American law, and comically useless inside a sealed iron cell.

Latin, roughly 'moving in the moving thing'. Aronnax insists the 'in' means within: the motto describes a vessel that moves inside the sea, not on top of it. Engraved on every piece of tableware, it is his first clue to the people on board.

Two of the most luxurious hotels of the day: the Adelphi in Liverpool, where transatlantic passengers stayed before sailing, and the Grand Hotel in Paris, opened in 1862 near the new Opéra. The comparison tells you the meal is anything but prison food.

Aronnax's chemistry is sound: heating potassium chlorate releases oxygen, and potassium hydroxide soaks up exhaled carbon dioxide. Versions of both tricks are still used today in submarines and spacecraft. His worry is that the chemicals would have to come from land.
notes.quote: releasing the oxygen contained in potassium chlorate

notes.text: Victorians believed the bracing smell of the seaside came from iodine and was good for the health. In fact the smell comes mostly from sulfur compounds given off by plankton and seaweed.

Buccaneers were the 17th-century pirates of the Caribbean. Navies hanged pirates and mutineers from a yardarm, the horizontal spar that holds a sail, in full view of the crew. Ned assumes that is how such adventures end.

Latin for 'no one', as the editor's note says. Classically minded readers would think of Homer's Odyssey, where Odysseus tells the Cyclops his name is 'Nobody'. The name hides a man while announcing that he is hiding.

The nautilus is a sea mollusk, and the 'paper nautilus' was long believed to sail on the surface using its arms as sails. The name also had a history in engineering: Robert Fulton's experimental submarine of 1800, built for France, was called Nautilus.
In Greek myth the Sphinx killed travelers who could not solve her riddle; Oedipus answered it and freed Thebes. Aronnax faces Nemo as a dangerous riddle he must somehow read.
A sea god of Greek myth, the 'old man of the sea', who herded the seals of Poseidon (Neptune) and could change shape at will. Nemo pictures himself as a shepherd of the ocean's flocks.
A soft, sausage-shaped relative of the starfish that lives on the seabed. Dried, as trepang or bêche-de-mer, it was a prized delicacy traded across Southeast Asia and China, hence the 'Malaysian'.

The ancient Phoenicians made 'Tyrian purple' from the glands of murex sea snails; thousands of snails yielded a gram of dye, so purple cloth became the color of emperors. Nemo dresses his guests the way Rome dressed its rulers.
notes.quote: dyed with purple ink from the murex snail

notes.text: The filaments are byssus, the silky threads with which the Mediterranean fan mussel (pen shell) anchors itself to rocks. Since antiquity small amounts were woven into a rare golden-brown cloth, as Aronnax explains to Conseil.
notes.quote: the masses of filaments that anchor certain seashells

notes.text: Literally 'plant-animals': an old category for creatures that seem halfway between the two, such as corals, sponges, sea anemones and, in Cuvier's scheme, starfish and sea urchins. Science has since dropped the group, but Aronnax uses it constantly.

A genus of brown seaweeds, the wracks found on northern rocky shores; Verne uses the word loosely for big seaweeds in general. They contain a sweet substance, mannitol, which is the 'sugar' on Nemo's table.
notes.quote: sugar from the huge fucus plants

notes.text: The shelf is a who's who of 19th-century science: Alexander von Humboldt, the explorer-geographer; Michael Faraday and John Tyndall, physicists of electricity and heat; Louis Agassiz, the Swiss-American naturalist; Léon Foucault of the pendulum. Their presence shows the captain's interests are physics and the sea.

Matthew Fontaine Maury (1806–1873), US Navy officer and founder of oceanography, whose wind and current charts shortened voyages worldwide. A Virginian, he sided with the Confederacy in the Civil War and went into exile afterward, which is the ruined career Aronnax mentions.

The list runs from Renaissance masters (Raphael, Leonardo, Titian) through Dutch and Spanish painters of the 1600s (Rubens, Velázquez, Murillo) to living French artists such as Delacroix, Ingres and Meissonier. Genuine works by all of them would have been worth a fortune.
notes.quote: a Raphael Madonna, a Virgin by Leonardo da Vinci

notes.text: The legendary singer of Greek myth whose music charmed even the gods of the underworld when he went down to bring back his dead wife. Nemo's point is that to the dead, all musicians are equally ancient.

Alongside Mozart, Haydn and Beethoven are the stars of 19th-century opera: Weber, Rossini, Meyerbeer, Gounod, and lesser Parisian favorites such as Hérold, Auber and Massé. Wagner was then the controversial modern; the piano-organ is a reed or pipe organ combined with a piano.
notes.quote: sheet music by Weber, Rossini, Mozart, Beethoven

notes.text: The giant clam (Tridacna) of the Indo-Pacific can exceed a meter across. Two of its shells, given to King François I by Venice, really do serve as holy-water basins in the Paris church of Saint-Sulpice. Nemo's is bigger still.
notes.quote: the Church of Saint-Sulpice in Paris

notes.text: 20,000 francs for one shell was what a skilled French worker might earn in fifteen or twenty years. Jean-Baptiste Tavernier was a 17th-century French gem merchant famous for his travels in Persia and India; a pearl worth 3,000,000 francs is a royal treasure.
notes.quote: whose value I estimated at 20,000 francs

notes.text: Small glossy cowry shells, mostly from the Maldives, served as everyday currency across India and much of West Africa for centuries, still in use in the 1860s.
notes.quote: every variety of cowry used as money

notes.text: The two keys to finding a ship's position. A sextant measures the sun's height at noon, which gives latitude. A chronometer, a very accurate clock set to the time at a home meridian, gives longitude: every four minutes' difference between local noon and home time means one degree.
notes.quote: chronometers, which allow me to calculate my longitude

notes.text: A sealed glass tube of chemicals in alcohol whose crystals were believed to change shape before bad weather; Admiral FitzRoy of the Beagle promoted it. It was popular in the 1860s but doesn't actually forecast anything.

In 1867 electricity powered the telegraph, arc lights and laboratory experiments, but no practical electric motor could drive a vehicle; the first good dynamos were only just being built. A ship lit, heated and driven at fifty miles per hour by electricity was pure, dazzling speculation. The fastest liners managed about fifteen.

Real devices of the day. The Bunsen cell (1841), invented by the German chemist Robert Bunsen, was a powerful zinc-and-carbon battery. Heinrich Ruhmkorff, a German instrument-maker in Paris, built the induction coil that turns battery current into high voltage. Nemo's swap of sodium for zinc is Verne's invention.
notes.quote: I use Bunsen cells, not Ruhmkorff cells

notes.text: Traditional Italian timekeeping counted the hours from one to twenty-four, starting at sunset, instead of two runs of twelve. Nemo's twenty-four-hour dial suits a place with no day or night.

Tanks that are flooded to make a vessel heavier, so it sinks, and pumped out to make it rise. Nemo's arithmetic of displacement and buoyancy is essentially how real submarines work. His fins, which steer the boat up and down, are what modern designers call diving planes.
notes.quote: These ballast tanks exist within easy access

notes.text: Real industrial giants of the 1860s: Schneider's ironworks at Le Creusot in France; Krupp of Essen, the Prussian steel and cannon-maker; Laird's of Birkenhead near Liverpool, which had built the Confederate raider Alabama; Scott's of Glasgow; the Motala works in Sweden. Ordering from all of them under false names is plausible industrial secrecy.
notes.quote: Its keel was forged by Creusot in France

notes.text: In 1867 two million francs would build a warship and four or five million was a great fortune. Paying off France's ten-billion-franc national debt alone would have taken the whole government's revenue for several years, so Nemo's boast is staggering.
Metric units. A myriameter is 10 kilometers (now obsolete), so a square myriameter is 100 square kilometers. A hectare is 10,000 square meters, about two and a half acres.

A geological period roughly 440 to 420 million years ago, named after an ancient Welsh tribe. Geologists of the 1860s pictured a molten 'era of fire' followed by a world-ocean from which continents slowly rose; the outline is roughly right, though the details have changed.

French navigators measured longitude from the Paris Observatory, about 2°20′ east of Greenwich. Since sailors kept chronometers set to their own country's meridian, Aronnax hopes the choice will betray Nemo's nationality. Nemo has clocks for Paris, Greenwich and Washington.
notes.quote: west of the meridian of Paris

notes.text: Galileo Galilei, the astronomer forced by the Inquisition in 1633 to recant his view that the earth moves around the sun, and kept under house arrest for the rest of his life: the classic scientist punished by society.

Great warm currents that flow like rivers through the ocean. The Gulf Stream runs from the Gulf of Mexico across the Atlantic; the Kuroshio ('black current' in Japanese, from its deep blue color) runs north past Japan. Maury had charted both.
notes.quote: the Kuroshio of the Japanese, the Black Current

notes.text: The Musée de Cluny in Paris, built on Alexandre du Sommerard's huge collection of medieval and Renaissance objects, crammed into an old abbots' mansion. Conseil compares the lounge to that famously packed treasure-house.

Conseil recites Cuvier's classification of fish from the 1810s, with Latin numbering (primo, secundo, tertio: first, second, third). Much of it is long outdated, though putting sharks and rays together has survived. Ned's 'fish we eat and fish we don't' is the rival system.
notes.quote: Bony fish are subdivided into six orders

notes.text: Green and hawksbill turtle soup was a prized luxury at 19th-century banquets, so much that live turtles were shipped to Europe to be cooked. The hawksbill, also killed for its 'tortoiseshell', is now critically endangered.
notes.quote: turtle soup made from the daintiest hawksbill

notes.text: The officer's morning phrase is in the crew's private language, the same one Aronnax failed to place earlier. The words match no known language, so for now it is simply part of the ship's mystery.

A speck marked on 19th-century charts of the North Pacific, supposedly sighted by a Captain Crespo in 1801. Like many 'phantom islands' of the old charts, it turned out not to exist and was later removed from maps.
notes.quote: Rocca de la Plata, in other words, “Silver Rock.”

notes.text: By the 1860s divers wore a waterproof canvas suit and a copper helmet, fed with air pumped down a hose from the surface, a design perfected by Augustus Siebe in the 1830s–40s. It worked, but the hose tied the diver to his boat, which is Nemo's objection.
notes.quote: That’s the standard equipment for a diving suit

notes.text: A real French invention patented in 1864–65 by the mining engineer Benoît Rouquayrol and the naval officer Auguste Denayrouze: a backpack tank with a regulator that released air as the diver breathed. Verne lets Nemo cut the surface hose entirely, anticipating the scuba gear of the 1940s.
A real portable electric lamp of the 1860s, used in mines: a battery and induction coil made a gas-filled glass tube glow. With no flame, it could not ignite mine gas, or go out underwater.

The earliest device for storing an electric charge (a capacitor), invented at Leyden in Holland in 1745: a glass jar coated with metal foil inside and out. Nemo's bullets are tiny ones that discharge on impact.
Dulse, a red seaweed long eaten in Ireland, Scotland, Iceland and Atlantic Canada. A liquor brewed from it is one of Verne's touches of real but exotic seafood lore.
notes.quote: the seaweed known by name as Rhodymenia palmata

notes.text: A floating colony of tiny animals that looks like a jellyfish, with a gas-filled blue float like a sail and stinging tentacles trailing many meters below. Its sting is extremely painful to swimmers.

Aronnax's science is partly off. Water absorbs red light first, so at 100 meters divers see a dim blue, not a 'reddish twilight'. Red algae can grow deeper than greens or browns, not in a middle band. He is right that sound travels about four times faster in water than in air.
notes.quote: a reddish twilight, a midpoint between day and night

notes.text: Seaweeds and their microscopic relatives. Verne's 500-meter fucus is an exaggeration: the giant kelp of the Pacific, the longest seaweed, reaches about 45–60 meters, which is still big enough to form true underwater forests.
notes.quote: fucus plants been gathered that were over 500 meters long

notes.text: In the 1860s helmet divers fed by air hoses rarely worked deeper than about 40 to 60 meters, so a walk at 150 meters is pure fantasy. Aronnax also guesses that sunlight cannot reach below about 150 meters. That is roughly right for useful light, though a faint glow reaches somewhat deeper in clear water.

Rising too fast after breathing compressed air lets dissolved gas form bubbles in the blood and joints. Today this is called decompression sickness, or the bends. In Verne's day it was being noticed in divers and in workers in pressurized caissons building bridge foundations, but nobody yet understood the cause.

A North Pacific otter that lives almost entirely at sea and has the densest fur of any animal. Russian, American and British hunters killed it by the hundred thousand for the fur markets of China and Russia. By the early 1900s it was nearly extinct, as Aronnax fears. His figure of 2,000 francs for one pelt was several years' wages for a French laborer.

The largest of the ocean-wandering seabirds. The wandering albatross has a wingspan of over three meters and can glide for days without landing. Sailors thought killing one brought bad luck, an idea made famous by Coleridge's poem The Rime of the Ancient Mariner (1798).
notes.quote: an albatross of the finest species

notes.text: A slim, deep-blue shark of the open ocean, common worldwide. It can attack people but rarely does. The glowing matter around the snout is Verne's touch. The pores on a shark's snout are actually sense organs that detect electric fields.

A large bag-shaped net dragged behind a boat. A wooden beam holds the mouth open and a weighted chain keeps the lower edge on the bottom. Normandy fishermen used this 'beam trawl.' Towed behind the Nautilus, it keeps the ship supplied with food and gives Aronnax endless specimens.

Nemo is explaining what drives deep currents: cold, salty water is heavy and sinks, and warm water rises. This is broadly true. His detail is off, though. Fresh water is densest at about 4°C, which is why lakes freeze from the top. Ordinary seawater simply gets denser as it cools until it freezes at about −1.9°C.
notes.quote: reach maximum density at -2 degrees centigrade

notes.text: A nineteenth-century catch-all name for the microscopic creatures found in water: single-celled organisms, larvae, tiny algae. The name comes from their turning up in 'infusions' of hay or leaves left in water. Today we would mostly say plankton. Nemo credits them with building coral and limestone, which mixes real science with guesswork.

Depths were measured by letting down a weighted line until it touched bottom, slow and unreliable work in deep water. The record South Atlantic depths Aronnax quotes, over 14,000 meters, were errors caused by currents carrying the line sideways. The deepest point in the Atlantic is about 8,400 meters. The ocean's average depth is about 3,700 meters, not seven kilometers.

In 1868 this was an independent kingdom with its own king, not yet part of the United States. Captain James Cook, Britain's greatest Pacific explorer, was killed in a fight with islanders at Kealakekua Bay on the Big Island in 1779. Mauna Kea is actually about 4,200 meters high, not 5,000.
notes.quote: where the famous Captain Cook met his death

notes.text: A group of steep volcanic islands in the South Pacific that France claimed in 1842. They are now part of French Polynesia. Nuku Hiva is the main island; Herman Melville had jumped ship there in 1842 and wrote about it in his novel Typee. Aronnax is pleased to see the French flag so far from home.

A French teacher and champion of free public schooling (1815–1894). The Servants of the Stomach (1866) explained digestion to young readers in friendly, storytelling style. Macé worked with Verne's own publisher, Hetzel, on a magazine that serialized this novel, so the mention is a small friendly plug.

The heavy ropes running from a mast down to the ship's sides that hold the mast upright. A ship that 'lists to port' is leaning to its left side. In a storm a crew might chop down the masts to keep the ship from capsizing, which is why the wreck has only stumps left.

A port on the north-east coast of England, at the mouth of the River Wear. In the nineteenth century it was one of the largest shipbuilding towns in the world. A ship's home port was painted on its stern beneath its name, which is how Aronnax can identify the wreck.

A long chain of low coral atolls in the South Pacific, now part of French Polynesia. The French navigator Louis-Antoine de Bougainville, who sailed round the world in 1766–69, called them the Dangerous Archipelago. They barely rise above the waves, so ships often ran onto them before sighting land.

A ring of coral reef or low islands around a lagoon. Aronnax gives the three classic reef types. A fringing reef hugs a coast. A barrier reef runs parallel to a coast with a lagoon behind it. An atoll is a ring with no central island at all.

In 1842 Charles Darwin argued that atolls begin as fringing reefs around volcanic islands. As the island slowly sinks, the coral keeps growing upward toward the light, until only a ring of reef is left. Many scientists of the day preferred the idea that coral simply capped underwater peaks. Drilling in the 1950s proved Darwin right.
notes.quote: the theory of Mr. Charles Darwin

notes.text: Reef-building stony corals. Each is a colony of tiny polyps, small soft animals related to sea anemones, which build limestone skeletons around themselves. Over thousands of years those skeletons pile up into reefs and islands. Precious red coral, used for jewelry, belongs to a different group.
notes.quote: Madrepores, which one must guard against confusing with precious coral

notes.text: Genesis describes God making the world in six days. A literal reading made the earth only about 6,000 years old. By the 1860s geology pointed to vastly longer ages. Aronnax takes a common position for believing scientists of the time: the biblical 'days' must mean long epochs, since the sun itself appears only on the fourth day.

Jean-François de La Pérouse led a French scientific voyage round the world from 1785, meant to rival Captain Cook's. His two ships were last seen leaving Botany Bay, Australia, in 1788, and their fate was one of the great mysteries of the age. Searches by d'Entrecasteaux failed. In 1826–27 the trader Peter Dillon found relics that tied the wrecks to Vanikoro, and Dumont d'Urville confirmed the site in 1828. In French the ships were La Boussole and L'Astrolabe; this translation calls the first the Compass.

Jules Dumont d'Urville (1790–1842), France's leading explorer of the Pacific. He made three great voyages and mapped much of Oceania. In 1828 his ship, renamed the Astrolabe in honor of La Pérouse, found the wreck site at Vanikoro and put up a memorial there. Earlier, in 1820, he had helped France acquire the newly found Venus de Milo.

An island chain in the south-west Pacific, named by Captain Cook in 1774. Britain and France ruled it jointly from 1906, and in 1980 it became the independent nation of Vanuatu. Vanikoro and Tikopia, which Verne lumps in with it, actually belong to the Santa Cruz group, now part of the Solomon Islands.
notes.quote: the island group of the New Hebrides

notes.text: Everything Aronnax tells up to the 1828 memorial is real history. Nemo's ending, with the escape boat lost in the Solomons and the tin box of orders, is Verne's invention. In real life the last survivors' fate has never been settled. One true detail: Louis XVI personally wrote notes in the margins of La Pérouse's instructions.
notes.quote: in the handwriting of King Louis XVI

notes.text: Red coral, the kind used for jewelry and beads since ancient times, mostly gathered in the Mediterranean. People long argued whether coral was a mineral, a plant or an animal. The Marseilles doctor Jean-André Peyssonnel showed in the 1720s that it is an animal; 1694, Verne's date, was the year he was born.

In June 1770 Cook's ship Endeavour struck what is now called Endeavour Reef, part of the Great Barrier Reef off north-east Australia. When the ship was beached for repairs, the crew found a lump of coral stuck in the hole, which had kept her from sinking. The Great Barrier Reef is the world's largest reef system, about 2,300 km long.
notes.quote: that daunting shoal where Captain Cook’s ships wellnigh miscarried

notes.text: The channel, about 150 km wide, between the northern tip of Australia (Queensland) and New Guinea. It is crowded with reefs and islets. The Spanish navigator Luis Vaez de Torres sailed through it in 1606. Charts were still poor in 1868, and it was one of the most feared passages for sailing ships.

Another name for New Guinea, the world's second-largest island, just north of Australia. In 1868 the Dutch claimed its western half on paper, and most of the island was unexplored by Europeans. Today it is divided between Indonesia and the independent nation of Papua New Guinea.

The Andaman Islands lie in the Bay of Bengal, thousands of kilometers from New Guinea. Verne's phrase is a slip. Nineteenth-century writers often lumped together the dark-skinned peoples of the Pacific and Indian Oceans. The islanders of the Torres Strait are Papuan and Melanesian peoples.

Tides are raised mainly by the moon's pull. At full moon and new moon, the sun and moon line up and their pulls add together, giving the highest high tides of the month, called spring tides (nothing to do with the season). Nemo is counting on the full moon of January 9 to float his ship off the reef.
notes.quote: in five days the moon will be full

notes.text: Pandanus trees, common on tropical shores. They stand on stilt-like prop roots, and their long leaves grow in a spiral, like the thread of a screw. Pacific islanders weave the leaves into mats and sails.

A large, starchy tropical fruit that is roasted or baked and tastes something like fresh bread or potato. It was so valued as cheap food that Britain sent Captain Bligh to carry breadfruit plants from Tahiti to the West Indies to feed enslaved workers. That voyage ended in the famous mutiny on the Bounty in 1789. Artocarpus is its scientific name.

In Verne's French, Malaisie means the whole Malay Archipelago: the islands of modern Indonesia, the Philippines and nearby, sometimes stretching to New Guinea. It does not mean the modern country of Malaysia. 'Malaysians' here are the peoples of those islands, and words like pisang (banana) are Malay.

The island group east of Madagascar in the Indian Ocean: Réunion, which is French, plus Mauritius and Rodrigues, which were British in 1868. French colonists brought useful tropical plants such as breadfruit there from the Pacific.

A starch taken from the soft pith inside the trunk of the sago palm. It is the staple food of many peoples in New Guinea and the Moluccas. The trunk is split, and the pith is pounded and washed so the flour settles out. Dried sago pearls were also sold in Europe for puddings.

Birds of New Guinea and nearby islands, famous for the males' spectacular plumes. Traders cut off the feet of the skins they sold, so early Europeans believed the birds had no legs and floated forever in paradise. Their feathers were in great demand for women's hats. Aronnax's 'great emerald' is the greater bird of paradise.

The seed of an evergreen tree native to the Banda Islands near New Guinea. Nutmeg was once worth more than its weight in gold, and the Dutch fought brutally to control its trade. Large fruit pigeons really do swallow nutmegs whole. A big dose of nutmeg can make a person intoxicated, which is the basis of Conseil's joke about the drunken bird.
notes.quote: Nutmeg, on which these birds habitually gorge themselves

notes.text: New Guinea shares many animals with Australia, because during the Ice Ages the two were joined by dry land where the Torres Strait now lies. The island has small wallabies and even tree-climbing kangaroos. These are marsupials, which carry their young in a pouch. Conseil's 'aplacental' means they lack the placenta most mammals use to nourish young in the womb.

Europeans of Verne's day routinely called tribal peoples 'savages' and assumed they were cannibals. Aronnax and his friends share these attitudes. It is Nemo who challenges them, asking whether so-called savages are any worse than men elsewhere. Some peoples of New Guinea did practice ritual cannibalism into the twentieth century, but European accounts greatly exaggerated it.

The five black keys of a piano form a pentatonic, or five-note, scale. Many Scottish and Irish folk tunes use this scale, as do folk musics in Asia and elsewhere. That is why a melody played only on the black keys sounds Scottish to Aronnax's ear.

Almost all snail shells coil the same way, clockwise when seen from the tip. Shells that coil the other way, called sinistral, are rare freaks in most species. Collectors paid fortunes for them, and in India a left-coiling conch was sacred. Aronnax's claim that the stars and the whole natural world share one 'handedness' is not real science.

Boats hollowed out of a single tree trunk. The bamboo poles Aronnax describes are an outrigger: a float fixed alongside on booms so the narrow hull does not capsize. Outrigger canoes let Pacific peoples settle islands across thousands of kilometers of open ocean.

In May 1842 Dumont d'Urville, his wife and his son died in France's first great railway disaster, near Meudon outside Paris. A train left the rails and caught fire, and passengers burned to death because the carriage doors were locked from outside. Death in a train wreck after a lifetime of surviving storms and reefs struck people of the time as a cruel irony.
notes.quote: perish wretchedly in a train wreck

notes.text: A stretch of the Antarctic coast that Dumont d'Urville sighted in 1840 and named after his wife, Adèle. The Adélie penguin takes its name from it. The Louis-Philippe Peninsula, named for the French king of the time, is part of the Antarctic Peninsula.

Latin for 'a sick man's dreams.' The phrase comes from the Roman poet Horace's Art of Poetry, where it describes wild, disordered images. It suits a chapter that ends with drugged sleep and hallucinations.
To 'double' a cape is to sail around it and change direction on the other side. Sailors speak of doubling the Cape of Good Hope or Cape Horn the same way.

The large, shallow bay cutting into northern Australia, between Arnhem Land and Cape York. Cape Wessel marks its north-western corner. It was named by Dutch explorers in the 1600s after Pieter de Carpentier, a governor of the Dutch East Indies.

An island north-west of Australia, then split between Dutch and Portuguese rule and governed locally by rajahs, or kings. A Timorese legend says the island itself is the body of a giant crocodile, and crocodiles were honored as ancestors, sometimes called 'grandfather.' Verne's maidens fed to crocodiles is a lurid traveler's tale.

Noctiluca, meaning 'night light', is a single-celled sea creature, nicknamed sea sparkle, that flashes blue-green when disturbed. Huge blooms make breaking waves and ships' wakes glow. Many jellyfish and other animals produce light too. The general name for living light is bioluminescence.
notes.quote: of noctiluca an eighth of an inch wide

notes.text: Ancient and medieval writers, beginning with Aristotle and Pliny, claimed the salamander could live in fire without burning. Alchemists made it the spirit of fire. Aronnax borrows the image for fish swimming unharmed through glowing water.

The European name for the Mediterranean coast of North Africa, from Morocco to Libya, after its Berber peoples. Its coral beds, especially off Algeria and Tunisia, were fished by Italian and French boats. At 500 francs a kilogram, the best coral cost more than a French worker earned in a year.

In the 1860s socialism, the idea of shared ownership and communal life, was a hot political topic in France, and Marx's Capital had just appeared in 1867. Aronnax's quip compares coral polyps to a commune: each animal lives its own life but shares a common skeleton and food supply.

The fan mussel, or pen shell, is a large Mediterranean shellfish that anchors itself with fine golden threads. Those threads were spun and woven into 'sea silk,' a rare, shimmering cloth made since ancient times in Sardinia and southern Italy. Nemo's crew use it for their clothing, and here for a burial shroud.

Pierre Gratiolet, an anatomist who studied the brain, and Alfred Moquin-Tandon, a botanist and zoologist, were respected French naturalists of the time. Both had trained in medicine. Many nineteenth-century naturalists began as doctors, as Aronnax did, because medicine was the main route into scientific training.
A heavy digging tool like a pickaxe, with one blade for breaking up hard ground and another for chopping. Here it is used to cut a grave in the limestone seafloor.

A navigator's instrument for measuring the angle of the sun or a star above the horizon. Taken at noon, the sun's height gives the ship's latitude. Combined with an accurate clock, it gives longitude too. This is the 'position fix' the chief officer takes every day.

The brightest electric light of Verne's day. Current jumps between two carbon rods, the 'graphite points,' and makes a dazzling arc of light. Arc lamps were first used in lighthouses around 1858. The rods burned away quickly in air, which is why Aronnax admires Nemo's vacuum, his own invention.

A tropical sea turtle whose beautiful mottled shell plates were the 'tortoiseshell' of combs, spectacles and inlaid furniture. That trade drove it close to extinction. It is now critically endangered and protected worldwide.

Two of the most modern rifles of the 1860s. The Chassepot was the French army's new breech-loading rifle, adopted in 1866. The Remington was an American design sold to armies around the world. The archerfish, which knocks insects off leaves with a jet of water, gets a weapon neither inventor dreamed of.

The Cocos (Keeling) Islands, a remote coral atoll in the eastern Indian Ocean, now an Australian territory. Charles Darwin and Captain FitzRoy visited it aboard the Beagle in 1836. Darwin's studies there helped shape his theory of how atolls form.

The P&O, a British steamship company founded in 1837. It carried mail and passengers between Britain, Egypt, India, the Far East and Australia. Its liners were the main link of the British Empire in the East. A steamer still carried masts and sails as a backup to its engines.

A small open-ocean octopus; the female grows a paper-thin spiral shell to hold her eggs. Aristotle and Pliny claimed it sailed the sea with two arms raised as sails, a charming myth that Aronnax repeats. The chambered nautilus, whose name Nemo's ship bears, is a different animal with a heavy, many-chambered shell.
notes.quote: now known by the name argonaut

notes.text: India's sacred river flows into the Bay of Bengal. Hindus consider it holy, and the ashes or bodies of the dead are committed to its waters, especially at the holy city of Benares (Varanasi). Bodies of the poor, who could not afford wood for a full cremation, were sometimes carried downstream to the sea.
notes.quote: Carried by the Ganges to the high seas

notes.text: Sailors had long reported nights when the whole sea glowed a steady white to the horizon. Scientists doubted these stories until a satellite photographed a milky sea in the Arabian Sea in 1995. The likely cause is vast numbers of glowing bacteria, rather than Aronnax's infusoria.

The island off India's southern tip, called Sri Lanka since 1972. In 1868 it was a British colony famous for its pearls, gems, coffee and cinnamon. H. C. Sirr's book, Ceylon and the Cingalese (1850), was a real travel account.

The shallow sea between north-western Ceylon and the southern tip of India. Its pearl beds were fished from ancient times. Under British rule the fishery was a government monopoly, held for a few weeks each spring when thousands of divers and traders gathered on the beaches.
A short-lived peace between Britain and Napoleon's France signed in 1802. Under it Britain kept Ceylon, which it had taken from the Dutch in 1796, and so gained the pearl fisheries.

From an Arabic word meaning 'unbeliever'. Europeans used it for black Africans, especially in southern Africa. It is now a grave racial slur. Nemo is citing Robert Percival's Account of the Island of Ceylon (1803).
notes.quote: a Kaffir who stayed under five minutes

notes.text: An old medical term for a sudden collapse with loss of consciousness, usually a stroke or brain hemorrhage. For breath-hold divers, the cause would often be blackout from lack of oxygen.

Jewelers' terms for a pearl's beauty. 'Water' is its translucent luster and color, and 'orient' is the soft rainbow shimmer on its surface. The best pearls are perfectly round or pear-shaped. Tiny seed pearls were sold by measure rather than one by one.

The Roman historian Suetonius records that Julius Caesar gave his mistress Servilia, mother of his later assassin Brutus, a pearl costing six million sesterces. It was a byword for extravagant love gifts.
notes.quote: Julius Caesar gave Servilia a pearl

notes.text: Pliny the Elder tells how Cleopatra bet Mark Antony she could spend ten million sesterces on one dinner. She dissolved one of her great pearl earrings in vinegar and drank it. Chemists doubt vinegar could dissolve a pearl that quickly, but the story became the classic example of wasteful luxury.
Holy Roman Emperor and King of Spain (reigned 1516–1556). Under him Spain exploited rich pearl beds off Venezuela and Panama, using Indigenous and enslaved African divers in brutal conditions.
notes.quote: during the reign of King Charles V

notes.text: A shiny paste made from the scales of the bleak, a small European river fish of the carp family. Coated inside hollow glass beads, it produced convincing imitation pearls. The technique was a French invention of the 1600s.

An island chain in the Bay of Bengal, home to Indigenous peoples who had long resisted outsiders. In 1858 Britain set up a penal colony there for Indian rebels. European writers of the day attached many fearsome legends to the islanders.
The French word for shark. The popular story that it comes from requiem, the Mass for the dead, is a folk etymology; its true origin is uncertain. Aronnax enjoys the gloomy pun anyway.
notes.quote: the French word for shark, requin

notes.text: The sailor who steers a ship's boat and commands its rowers, from the stern. The tiller is the handle that turns the rudder. A thwart is a crosswise bench in a rowing boat where the oarsmen sit.
notes.quote: The longboat’s coxswain took the tiller

notes.text: Tridacna, the largest living shellfish, found on Indo-Pacific reefs; it can exceed a meter across and 200 kg. Huge shells were brought to Europe as curiosities. The church of Saint-Sulpice in Paris still uses two as holy-water fonts, a gift to King Francis I from Venice, which is why Aronnax makes the comparison.
The giant hero of François Rabelais's comic novels of the 1530s, famous for his colossal appetite. The word 'gargantuan' comes from him.

The world's largest land crab, found on Indian Ocean and Pacific islands. Darwin described it at Keeling Island cracking coconuts with its huge claws. Despite Aronnax, adults live on land and would drown underwater.
notes.quote: the enormous crab that Mr. Darwin observed

notes.text: The plainest and sturdiest of the classical column styles, a simplified Roman version of the Greek Doric. Aronnax means the cave's natural pillars are thick, plain and massive.
notes.quote: the weighty columns of Tuscan architecture

notes.text: As early as the 1200s, Chinese farmers slipped tiny lead figures of the Buddha inside freshwater mussels, which coated them with mother-of-pearl. Aronnax imagines Nemo doing the same. Perfectly round cultured pearls were not mastered until the 1890s, in Japan.
notes.quote: following the examples of oyster farmers in China and India

notes.text: The old scientific name for the blacktip reef shark, named for the black tips of its fins. The real animal rarely tops two meters. Verne's twenty-five-foot monster is pure exaggeration, perhaps borrowed from an unreliable source.

In the 1860s a French laborer earned perhaps 3 to 5 francs a day, and a comfortable middle-class family lived on a few thousand a year. Ten million francs was a fortune beyond most kings' jewels. By contrast, the Ceylon divers got about a penny for each oyster with a pearl.

The narrow strait between Arabia and Africa that joins the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. Its Arabic name is usually translated 'Gate of Grief' or 'Gate of Tears,' for the dangers of its currents and reefs. Britain occupied Perim Island in the middle of it in 1857.
notes.quote: the Strait of Bab el Mandeb

notes.text: Ferdinand de Lesseps, a French diplomat, organized the digging of a canal across the desert isthmus of Suez to link the Mediterranean and the Red Sea. Work began in 1859. In February 1868, when this chapter takes place, it was still unfinished; it opened in November 1869, while Verne was writing the novel. It cut thousands of kilometers off the voyage from Europe to Asia.
notes.quote: the Isthmus of Suez hasn’t been cut all the way through yet

notes.text: A port on the Red Sea coast of Yemen. It was the world's great coffee market in the 1600s and 1700s, and gave its name to mocha coffee. By 1868 trade had moved elsewhere and the town was largely in ruins.

notes.term: why the Red Sea is red
notes.text: Nemo is right that blooms of a tiny blue-green alga, Trichodesmium, can stain the water reddish-brown. Many scholars think this gave the sea its ancient Greek name, Erythra Thalassa, 'red sea.' His Hebrew 'Edrom' is doubtful; the Hebrew Bible calls it Yam Suph, the Sea of Reeds.

In the Book of Exodus, Moses parts the sea so the Israelites can escape from Egypt on dry land, and the waters close over Pharaoh's pursuing army. Where this happened, if it did, has been debated for centuries. Nemo places it in the shallows just north of Suez.

Nemo's history is broadly accurate. Pharaoh Necho II began a canal from the Nile to the Red Sea around 600 BC. The Persian king Darius I and the Greek-Egyptian king Ptolemy II completed or restored it, and it was reopened and closed several times until an Abbasid caliph filled it in during the 760s. It connected the seas through the Nile, not directly across the isthmus as de Lesseps's canal does.

Napoleon Bonaparte invaded Egypt in 1798, bringing scholars as well as soldiers. In 1799 he visited Suez, looked for traces of the ancient canal, and was nearly drowned when the tide rose while he was crossing the shallows. His engineers wrongly concluded that the Red Sea stood ten meters higher than the Mediterranean, which delayed canal plans for decades.
Latin for 'they have ears but hear not,' from Psalm 115, where it mocks idols of wood and stone. Nemo turns it on people who refuse to believe what they have not seen.

Nemo's underground passage from Suez to the Mediterranean is Verne's invention; no such tunnel exists. His evidence, the same fish turning up in both seas, does have a real echo. Since the Suez Canal opened, hundreds of Red Sea species have migrated into the Mediterranean through it.
A small port on the Sinai shore of the Gulf of Suez, long a stop for pilgrims going to Mount Sinai and Mecca. Nemo says its bay can turn blood-red from tiny algae.
Jeddah, a port on the Red Sea coast of Arabia. It was the sea gateway for Muslim pilgrims travelling to Mecca, about 70 km inland, and a busy trading town. In 1868 it was under Ottoman rule.

A large, slow, plant-eating sea mammal of warm coastal waters, related to the manatee and, more distantly, to the elephant. Its order, Sirenia, is named after the sirens of Greek myth, because sailors' glimpses of these creatures may lie behind mermaid legends. Hunted for its meat, it is now protected and vulnerable to extinction.
Pronounced 'gunnel'. The upper edge of a boat's side. The stempost is the upright timber at the very front of the bow.

'Rocky Arabia', the old Roman name for the Sinai Peninsula and the lands around Petra. Ras Mohammed is the southern tip of Sinai, where the Red Sea splits into the Gulf of Suez to the west and the Gulf of Aqaba to the east.

In the Bible, Horeb and Sinai are names for the mountain where Moses received the Ten Commandments amid thunder and lightning. Tradition places it in the high mountains of southern Sinai, at the site of St. Catherine's Monastery.
A lightship: a vessel anchored at a fixed spot and carrying a beacon, used where building a lighthouse is impractical. The one off Suez marked the approach for ships heading to the new canal port.
Strictly, a deadlight is a heavy cover bolted over a porthole in bad weather. Here Verne uses the word for the thick glass windows of the wheelhouse.

An ancient Egyptian city at the easternmost mouth of the Nile, guarding the road between Egypt and Asia. It saw many battles, including the Persian conquest of Egypt in 525 BC. By Verne's time only ruins and marshes remained near the new canal.

The new town at the Mediterranean end of the Suez Canal, founded in 1859 and named after Egypt's ruler Said Pasha. Long stone jetties were built out to sea to keep sand from silting up the canal entrance.

In 1866 Greek Christians on Crete rose against the island's Ottoman Turkish rulers, hoping to join Greece. The revolt won wide sympathy in Europe, especially after defenders of Arkadi Monastery blew themselves up rather than surrender. It was crushed by 1869. Crete finally joined Greece in 1913.
notes.quote: in rebellion against its tyrannical rulers

notes.text: Verne borrows a famous southern Italian legend: Nicola Pesce, or Colapesce, 'Nicholas the Fish,' a youth from Sicily who spent so much time in the water that he became half fish. Verne moves him to Cape Matapan, the southern tip of mainland Greece. The Cyclades are the island group in the middle of the Aegean.

The remora, or suckerfish, has a suction disk on its head and hitches rides on sharks, turtles and ships. Its Latin name means 'delay.' Pliny claimed one held back Mark Antony's flagship at the Battle of Actium in 31 BC, where Octavian, later the emperor Augustus, defeated Antony and Cleopatra.

Roman emperor for a few months in AD 69, remembered chiefly as a glutton. Suetonius describes his giant platter, the 'Shield of Minerva,' heaped with fish livers, pheasant and peacock brains, flamingo tongues and lamprey roe gathered from across the empire.

Santorini, ancient Thera, is the ring-shaped remnant of a huge volcano in the southern Aegean. Its Bronze Age eruption around 1600 BC was one of the largest in human history. An eruption began in January 1866 at the central islet of Nea Kameni, and the new islets George, Aphroessa and Reka are real; it went on until 1870.
The Venetian and Italian name for Kythira, an island off the southern tip of the Peloponnese. In myth it is where Aphrodite came ashore after her birth from the sea foam.
Latin for 'our sea.' The Romans called the Mediterranean this because they ruled every shore of it. The phrase later became a slogan for anyone claiming to dominate the sea.

The Roman gods of the sea and of the underworld. Aronnax casts the Mediterranean as a battlefield between water and underground fire, meaning volcanoes and earthquakes, as at Etna, Vesuvius and Santorini. Geologists of the time called such forces 'plutonic.'

Working out a ship's position from its last known point, its compass heading, its speed and the time elapsed, without sighting land or stars. Errors build up over time, so navigators correct it with astronomical sights whenever they can.

A Roman general of the first century BC who retired rich from his eastern wars and became famous for his lavish banquets. 'Lucullan' still means sumptuous. He kept fishponds by the sea for luxury fish.

The sestertius was the Roman unit for counting money. A legionary soldier under Augustus earned about 900 sesterces a year, so 10,000 for a single red mullet was absurd extravagance. Roman writers grumbled about exactly such prices, and the color-changing death of a mullet really was a dinner-table show.

The Mediterranean monk seal, once common along these coasts and now one of the rarest seals in the world, with only a few hundred left. The Dominicans are an order of friars who wear a white habit with a black cloak, hence the joke about the seals' solemn black-and-white looks.
notes.quote: known by the name monk seals

notes.text: The channel between Sicily and Tunisia that divides the Mediterranean into eastern and western basins. A raised underwater ridge runs across it. The 'Smith' of the soundings is the British admiral William Henry Smyth, who surveyed the Mediterranean in the 1820s.

Aronnax gives the science of his day. Physicists such as Lord Kelvin reasoned that the earth was a hot ball slowly losing its inner heat and would one day be cold and dead like the moon. The discovery of radioactivity in 1896 showed the earth's interior is still heated by radioactive decay, which overturned that reasoning.
notes.quote: the heat inside the earth is growing weaker

notes.text: Aronnax reasons correctly. Atlantic water flows into the Mediterranean at the surface, while heavier, saltier Mediterranean water spills out into the Atlantic along the bottom. British scientists confirmed this deep outflow in 1870, a year after Verne wrote. In the Second World War submarines used it to slip silently through the strait.

The ancients called the two headlands at the Strait of Gibraltar the Pillars of Hercules, marking the edge of the known world. A famous temple to Hercules, the Phoenician god Melqart, stood near Gades, modern Cádiz. Legends told of ruins sunk beneath the waves.

The original name given to the Cape of Good Hope by the Portuguese explorer Bartolomeu Dias, who rounded the southern tip of Africa in 1488 after fierce storms. The Portuguese king renamed it to sound more hopeful. With Cape Horn, it was the most feared headland for sailing ships.

Any circle on a globe whose center is the center of the earth, such as the equator or a line of longitude. A great circle measures about 40,000 km, or 10,000 of the four-kilometer leagues Aronnax uses. So the Nautilus has already traveled the distance once around the world.
notes.quote: a great circle of the earth

notes.text: Tadeusz Kościuszko (1746–1817), a Polish-Lithuanian officer who fought for American independence and in 1794 led a Polish uprising against Russia. Legend says that when he fell wounded he cried 'Finis Poloniae', 'the end of Poland', though he denied it. Poland was then partitioned out of existence by its neighbors.

Three champions of national freedom. Markos Botsaris was a Greek independence leader killed in 1823 fighting the Ottomans. Daniel O'Connell, 'the Liberator,' won civil rights for Irish Catholics in 1829. Daniele Manin led Venice's short-lived republic against Austrian rule in 1848–49. Leonidas was the Spartan king who died holding the pass of Thermopylae against Persia.

Abraham Lincoln, who led the Union through the American Civil War (1861–65), was shot by the Confederate sympathizer John Wilkes Booth in April 1865, less than three years before this scene. John Brown led an armed raid on Harpers Ferry, Virginia, in 1859, hoping to spark a slave uprising, and was hanged. Victor Hugo begged for his life and then drew a haunting picture of him on the gallows.
notes.quote: that martyr for the redemption of the black race, John Brown

notes.text: When the childless King Charles II of Spain died in 1700, he left his throne to Louis XIV's grandson, who became Philip V. England, the Dutch Republic and Austria went to war (1701–1714) to stop France and Spain from uniting under one family, backing the Austrian Archduke Charles instead. Philip kept his throne in the end.

Large, heavily armed sailing ships. Each year Spain's treasure fleets of galleons carried silver and gold from its American colonies home across the Atlantic, and they were prime targets for enemy navies and pirates.
notes.quote: its galleons, laden with gold and silver from America

notes.text: A real battle of October 1702 in the bay of Vigo in north-western Spain. An Anglo-Dutch fleet smashed the French escort and the Spanish treasure ships. In fact much of the silver had already been unloaded, but legends of sunken millions drew treasure hunters to the bay for two centuries, including in Verne's own day.
The Spanish silver peso, worth eight reales, the most widely used coin in the world for three centuries. It is the treasure of pirate stories, and it was the model for the American dollar.

Spanish conquistadors seized the Americas' riches in the 1500s. Hernán Cortés conquered the Aztec Empire of Mexico in 1519–21, and Francisco Pizarro the Inca Empire of Peru from 1532. Their gold, and the vast silver mines worked by forced Indigenous labor, filled Spain's treasure fleets.

The sunken island empire described by Plato in his dialogues Timaeus and Critias (about 360 BC). Plato says the story reached Athens through the lawgiver Solon, who heard it from Egyptian priests at Sais: a great power beyond the Pillars of Hercules that made war on ancient Athens and vanished in a single day and night. Most scholars read it as a philosophical fable. In Verne's day, though, theories that it had really existed were popular, and Aronnax's long list of believers and doubters is a roll call of ancient and modern authorities.

A vast continent beyond the ocean invented by the Greek historian Theopompus of Chios (4th century BC). Its two cities were Machimos ("Warlike") and Eusebes ("Pious"), which is where Aronnax's "Makhimos" and "Eusebes" come from. The tale was probably a satire of Plato's Atlantis, but Aronnax takes it as supporting evidence.

The ancient name for the two headlands on either side of the Strait of Gibraltar: the Rock of Gibraltar and Jebel Musa in Morocco. For the Greeks they marked the edge of the known world, so "beyond the Pillars" meant out in the open Atlantic.

notes.term: Madeira, the Azores, the Canaries, the Cape Verde Islands
notes.text: Volcanic island groups in the Atlantic off Portugal and northwest Africa. Atlantis enthusiasts claimed them as the drowned continent's surviving mountaintops. The Atlantic floor really is volcanic, as Aronnax says, but the reason was only understood in the 1960s. Along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge the seafloor is slowly pulling apart and new crust is forming, and the Azores sit right on that ridge.
notes.quote: Madeira, the Azores, the Canaries, the Cape Verde Islands

notes.term: Pompeii, Vesuvius and Torre del Greco
notes.text: The Roman town of Pompeii was buried by an eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD 79. In the 1860s its excavation was front-page news, especially the plaster casts of victims made from 1863 onward. Torre del Greco is a town at the foot of Vesuvius that lava flows overran again and again, worst of all in 1794. To Verne's readers, "a whole Pompeii" meant an entire city preserved by catastrophe.
notes.quote: a whole Pompeii buried under the waters

notes.text: A long wooden staff with an iron point, used by climbers in the Alps. It was the forerunner of the ice axe and the trekking pole. Nemo hands Aronnax one because their night walk includes climbing a mountain.
notes.quote: an alpenstock being placed in my hand

notes.text: Prehistoric stone tombs made of upright stones roofed with a huge flat slab. They are especially common in Brittany and would have been familiar to any French reader as the oldest human buildings they knew.
notes.quote: like the dolmens of prehistoric times

notes.text: Triremes: oared warships of ancient Greece with three banks of rowers on each side and a bronze ram at the bow. They were the battleships of the Athenian navy, so Aronnax is picturing a port fit for the Atlanteans' war with Athens.

A headland on the easternmost bulge of Brazil, near Natal. Sailing ships bound from Europe for the Cape of Good Hope swung far west toward it to pick up favorable winds before turning southeast. That's why sails are on the horizon in mid-Atlantic.

Jean Sylvain Bailly (1736–1793), a French astronomer who wrote a book of letters about Atlantis in 1779, placing it in the far north (hence the editor's footnote). He became the first mayor of Paris during the Revolution and was guillotined in 1793.

The Nautilus runs on electricity from sodium batteries, as Nemo explained to Aronnax earlier in the voyage. Nemo extracts the sodium from seawater by heating it with coal. That explains the chain he recites (coal makes sodium, sodium feeds batteries, batteries make electricity) and why he needs a secret coal mine. Sodium really was produced with coal-fired furnaces in the 1860s.

Newcastle upon Tyne in northeast England was the most famous coal district in the world, which is why "carrying coals to Newcastle" means doing something pointless. Some of the region's mines really did run out under the North Sea, so Nemo's undersea mine has a real-world model.

Dracaena draco, a strange umbrella-shaped tree native to the Canary Islands and nearby Atlantic islands. Its red resin, called "dragon's blood", was sold as a dye and medicine. Together with the bees "so common to all the Canary Islands", it's Aronnax's clue to roughly where the volcano is.
notes.quote: a sturdy clump of dragon trees

notes.text: Conglomerate: rock made of rounded pebbles cemented together, like the fruit in a plum pudding. Here they're loose, which is why the climb is so treacherous. Tuff, trachyte and obsidian, also mentioned, are all rocks formed by volcanoes.

Basalt is dark volcanic rock. When a thick lava flow cools slowly, it can crack into regular six-sided pillars, as at the Giant's Causeway in Ireland or Fingal's Cave in Scotland. That's the "natural architecture" holding up the cavern's vault.

In Scott's novel The Antiquary (1816), Sir Arthur Wardour and his daughter Isabella are cut off by the incoming tide at the foot of sea cliffs and rescued at the last moment. It was one of the best-known scenes in 19th-century fiction.
Small fish that bury themselves in sand with only their venomous back spines showing. Stepping on one is agonizing, and swimmers on European beaches still get stung.
notes.quote: weevers known in Aristotle’s day as sea dragons

notes.text: The powerful warm current that flows out of the Gulf of Mexico, up the American coast and across the Atlantic toward Europe. It helps give northwest Europe its mild climate. Verne's description of its branches is a little muddled, but the basic idea is right: it's one side of a huge clockwise circulation of the North Atlantic.
notes.quote: known by name as the Gulf Stream

notes.text: A calm region of the North Atlantic east of Bermuda, ringed by currents and covered with floating mats of sargassum seaweed. It's the only sea with no coastline. The weed actually lives and grows at sea rather than being torn from distant beaches. In the 1920s scientists found that European and American eels travel here to spawn.

Columbus's ships reached the Sargasso weed in September 1492. His crews feared it meant hidden shallows, but they also took it as a sign that land was near. Aronnax's "three long weeks" exaggerates how much it slowed them.
The southern tip of South America, on a Chilean island. Its gales, huge waves and icebergs made it the most feared passage in the age of sail. To "double" a cape means to sail around it.

Ocean depth was measured by lowering a weighted line. Currents carried the line sideways, so it kept paying out without touching bottom. That's how Denham (HMS Herald) and Parker (USS Congress) reported 14,000–15,000 meters in the 1850s, figures now known to be wrong. The deepest point in the South Atlantic is about 8,300 meters, and the deepest anywhere, in the Pacific's Mariana Trench, is about 11,000. The Nautilus's 16,000-meter dive goes deeper than any real ocean.

A unit of pressure: one atmosphere is the weight of air at sea level, about 1 kilogram on every square centimeter. Water adds roughly one more atmosphere every 10 meters down. For comparison, the bathyscaphe Trieste, at the bottom of the Mariana Trench in 1960, faced about 1,100 atmospheres.

In Verne's day many naturalists believed that the deep ocean, below a few hundred fathoms, was lifeless (the "azoic" theory). In 1860 HMS Bulldog, surveying a route for a telegraph cable, hauled up starfish clinging to its line from more than 2,000 fathoms. That was some of the first hard evidence against the theory. (A fathom is six feet, about 1.8 meters.)

In 1868 photography meant glass plates and long exposures. The first underwater photograph was taken in 1856 by William Thompson in shallow water off southern England. A crisp picture of the abyssal floor was pure science fiction. Real ones came only in the 20th century.
notes.quote: taking a photograph of this underwater region

notes.text: The orca, which really is the largest member of the dolphin family. That's why Aronnax can call it a dolphin. It hunts seals, porpoises and even large whales. The "Copenhagen professor" is the Danish zoologist Daniel Eschricht, who reported the remains of over a dozen porpoises and seals in one orca's stomach.

Baleen whales have no teeth. They strain small creatures from the water through plates of "whalebone" (baleen) hanging from the upper jaw, which was valued for corsets and umbrella ribs. Sperm whales are toothed hunters that dive deep for squid. Nemo's contrast between "harmless" baleen whales and "cruel" sperm whales reflects the attitudes of his time.

A waxy oil filling a huge chamber in the sperm whale's head. It made the finest candles and lubricants and was the main reason sperm whales were hunted. The name ("whale seed") comes from an old belief that it was the whale's sperm.

Right whales got their name from whalers: they were the "right" whale to hunt because they swim slowly, stay near coasts and float when killed. By the 1860s they had been hunted to near-extinction. The bowhead Ned knows from the Arctic is a close relative. Aronnax's species distinctions are partly confused by modern standards.
notes.quote: the southern right whale is still unknown to you

notes.text: The Bering Strait separates Alaska from Siberia. The Davis Strait lies between Greenland and Baffin Island. Whalers hunted bowheads in both. Ned's harpooned whale really is evidence of an Arctic route linking the two, the way Aronnax suggests.
notes.quote: the Bering Strait and the Davis Strait

notes.text: A Nantucket whaleship rammed and sunk in the Pacific in November 1820. It was attacked by a sperm whale, not the baleen whale Aronnax describes. The survivors spent three months in open boats, some resorting to cannibalism. The disaster inspired Herman Melville's Moby-Dick (1851).

In the Arabian Nights, on Sinbad's first voyage, his crew land on a little island, light a fire and discover that it's a sleeping whale, which dives. The same legend appears in the medieval voyage of Saint Brendan. Aronnax is teasing Ned that his whale story is straight out of a fairy tale.
notes.quote: Like in the voyages of Sinbad the Sailor

notes.text: Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon (1707–1788), author of the 36-volume Natural History, the most widely read science book of the 18th century. By 1868 many of its claims, like whales living a thousand years, were badly out of date, which is Aronnax's point.
A jaunty American song from the Revolutionary War. Whistling it with his hands in his pockets is Ned's way of showing he's unimpressed by Nemo's lecture.

The Basques of northern Spain and southwest France were Europe's first commercial whalers. They hunted right whales in the Bay of Biscay from around the 11th century and crossed to Labrador by the 1500s, long before the English and Dutch joined in.
notes.quote: first dragged the Basques in its wake

notes.text: Whalers' slang for a herd (a "pod") of whales. It also meant a social visit between two whaling ships meeting at sea. Ned is using his old trade's vocabulary.

The translator's term for Verne's "banquise": the wall of pack ice, fused icebergs and ice shelves that surrounds Antarctica. In 1841 James Clark Ross met the Great Ice Barrier (now the Ross Ice Shelf), ice cliffs up to about 60 meters high. Sailing ships of Verne's day could push no farther, which is why Ned treats it as nature's final boundary.
A white glare on the underside of clouds, reflected from ice beyond the horizon. Polar sailors read it as a warning of pack ice ahead. The opposite, a dark "water sky", signaled open water.

notes.term: icebergs, ice fields, drift ice, packs
notes.text: The polar sailors' working vocabulary. Icebergs are floating mountains broken off glaciers. Ice fields are vast flat sheets of frozen sea. Drift ice is loose floating floes. Packs are jumbled broken ice crammed together. Conseil, the born classifier, is naturally delighted.

The line of latitude at about 66°33′ south. South of it the sun stays up for at least one full day at midsummer and stays down for at least one full day at midwinter. Only a handful of expeditions had crossed it by 1868.

notes.term: South Shetland and South Orkney Islands
notes.text: Bleak island groups off the tip of the Antarctic Peninsula, discovered around 1819–1821. British and American sealers stripped them of their fur seals within a few seasons, so Nemo's bitter account is historically accurate.
notes.quote: South Shetland and South Orkney Islands

notes.text: A compass points to the magnetic poles, which are not at the geographic poles and slowly wander. Near a magnetic pole the needle tries to point down into the earth and becomes useless for steering. Hansteen and Duperrey were scientists who estimated its position. A party from Shackleton's expedition first reached it in 1909.

Fresh water is densest at about 4 °C, so the coldest water rises and lakes freeze from the top down. Aronnax assumes seawater behaves the same way, but ocean water actually keeps getting denser right down to its freezing point. His conclusion still holds: the ice floats and the water beneath it stays liquid.

Nemo's three feet below for every foot above is too low. Because ice is about 90 percent as dense as seawater, roughly seven to nine times as much of an iceberg lies below the surface as above it. That's where "the tip of the iceberg" comes from.
notes.quote: For each foot of iceberg above the sea

notes.text: Many 19th-century geographers, Maury among them, believed in an "open polar sea": ice-free water at the poles, kept warm by ocean currents beyond a ring of ice. Arctic expeditions were launched to find it. It doesn't exist. The Arctic is a frozen ocean, and Antarctica is a continent buried under ice up to four kilometers thick.
notes.quote: why wouldn’t we find open sea at the South Pole

notes.text: In 1868 no one had come within about 1,300 kilometers of the South Pole. It was first reached overland by Roald Amundsen's Norwegian party on December 14, 1911, five weeks ahead of Robert Falcon Scott.
