He warns that if its speed or direction changed, Europe's climates would suffer "disturbances whose consequences are incalculable." Climate scientists today worry about exactly that weakening.

insights.title: Courting the lightning
insights.text: Nemo, who has hidden in his cabin since the squid attack, braves a hurricane lashed to the platform. He stares into the lightning as if he wanted to be struck, and the spur draws sparks like a lightning rod. Meanwhile Ned is in sight of his own country, the St. Lawrence, his river, and says he is suffocating. Both men are in torment, for different reasons.

insights.title: A battlefield of wrecks
insights.text: Off Newfoundland the seafloor is strewn with lost ships, and the Nautilus moves among them "as if passing the dead in review." Wrecks have marked the whole voyage: the Florida, La Pérouse's ships, the Vigo galleons. Each one shows the sea as a graveyard, and this chapter ends at the most deliberate grave of all.

insights.title: The Atlantic cable
insights.text: The transatlantic telegraph cable was brand new when Verne wrote. The Great Eastern finally landed a lasting one in 1866, after failed attempts in 1858 and 1865. Aronnax quotes its first message: "peace on earth to men of good will." Nemo's ship follows the thread that ties the nations together, back toward the shores he left.

insights.title: The Vengeur and its legend
insights.text: The ship is the real Vengeur du Peuple, sunk at the Battle of the Glorious First of June in 1794 between the French and British fleets. Revolutionary France made it a legend: a crew that went down rather than surrender, shouting "Long live the Republic!" In fact many of its men were rescued by the British. Nemo tells the legend and honors it on the anniversary.

insights.title: Why this grave?
insights.text: Nemo spends two days searching for one exact spot, works out the date in the French Revolutionary calendar, and murmurs over the name Avenger, "A splendid name!" Aronnax wonders whether being near Europe stirs remorse or regret. What does Nemo admire in this ship: the cause it served, its refusal to surrender, or its name?

insights.title: "I'm the law, I'm the tribunal"
insights.text: For the first time Nemo says what was done to him. His "oppressors" destroyed "homeland, wife, children, father, and mother." He makes himself judge, jury and executioner. The grievance Aronnax has guessed at for months is real and terrible, and in Nemo's mind it justifies sinking a ship with all hands.

insights.title: A nationality kept secret
insights.text: The warship flies no flag, Ned can't name its nation, and Nemo refuses to tell: "At least its nationality will remain a secret to you." The enemy stays blank, so the reader, like Aronnax, can only guess at the oppressor.

insights.title: The hunt turned around
insights.text: The book opened with warships hunting a "monster." Now one fires on the Nautilus because people know it is a machine with men inside. Aronnax looks back with new eyes at the night in the cell and the crewman buried in coral. The ship built for exploration is cleared for action and goes through the warship's hull "like a sailmaker's needle through canvas."

insights.title: "I stared—I too!"
insights.text: Locked below, Aronnax experiences the attack through sound alone. Then at the window he sees the drowning men, "a human anthill," and confesses he couldn't look away. Verne makes his narrator, and the reader, a horrified witness who can't stop watching. Aronnax had said he would rather perish with the ship than be an accomplice to revenge.

insights.title: Executioner and father
insights.text: The chapter ends in two images side by side. Nemo, "this true archangel of hate," watches the ship sink to the end. Then he kneels before a portrait of a young woman and two children and sobs. Verne doesn't ask us to choose between the two Nemos.

insights.title: The logbook goes blank
insights.text: For forty-five chapters Aronnax has given dates, depths and coordinates. After the massacre, positions stop appearing on the chart, the clocks seem to stop, and he can't say whether fifteen or twenty days pass. He compares himself to Poe's Arthur Gordon Pym. Verne admired Poe and had written an essay on him, and here his precise realism dissolves into a feverish dream.

insights.title: The Spirit of the Seas
insights.text: Lying awake before the escape, Aronnax replays the whole voyage like stage scenery, and Nemo swells into "the Man of the Waters, the Spirit of the Seas." On the walk to Atlantis he had called him a "Spirit of the Sea." What began as admiration now sounds closer to dread.

insights.title: "Enough! Enough!"
insights.text: Nemo's last words to reach Aronnax are a sob: "O almighty God! Enough! Enough!" Aronnax wonders whether it is a vow of repentance. Enough of what: the killing, the grief, his own life? The book gives his words and doesn't explain them.

insights.title: The Maelstrom
insights.text: The Maelstrom is a real tidal whirlpool in Norway's Lofoten Islands, made legendary by Poe's story "A Descent into the Maelström" (1841). Verne invokes it at the worst possible moment, just as the skiff is coming loose. Aronnax can't tell whether Nemo steered there "accidentally—or perhaps deliberately." Every human plan aboard is suddenly at the mercy of the sea.

insights.title: A last look at the museum
insights.text: Before leaving, Aronnax spends an hour among the treasures in the glass cases, a collection he expects to "perish someday in the depths of the seas, together with its curator." He packs his notes against his body. Even while running for his life, he holds on to what he has learned.

insights.title: The escape left blank
insights.text: How the skiff got out of the whirlpool, Aronnax says, "I'm unable to say." He wakes in a fisherman's hut with Ned and Conseil holding his hands. Verne skips the rescue entirely and keeps the three friends together at the end.

insights.title: Questions without answers
insights.text: Aronnax ends with a string of questions. Did the Nautilus survive? Is Nemo still taking revenge? Will the manuscript ever surface? Will the warship's nationality reveal Nemo's? The book refuses to answer them. "No one" stays no one.

insights.title: May the executioner pass away
insights.text: Aronnax's last wish is that the wonders of the sea will quiet the hate in "that fierce heart." He hopes the executioner will give way to the scientist. He calls the ocean Nemo's "adopted country," and with the words of Ecclesiastes he puts himself beside Nemo as one of only two men who can answer "Who can fathom the soundless depths?" He condemns the man and still feels bound to him.

insights.title: Will anyone believe me?
insights.text: Aronnax insists that not a fact has been omitted and not a detail exaggerated, then admits he doesn't know whether he'll be believed. He rests his authority on having seen it all: he has "earned the right to speak of these seas." The book closes the way it opened, with a scientist weighing evidence against disbelief.
